Former
for'mer
a. (before in time; the first of two; belonging to the past; rendering Hebrew rishon, Greek proteros)
A double comparative from forme, first, on the pattern of latter. Hebrew rishon is from rosh, the head, and means first or foremost — so the former things are the head of the sequence, what came before.

Biblical Definition

Former points backwards, and Scripture gives careful and sometimes surprising instructions about how to regard what lies there. Isaiah commands a startling forgetfulness: “Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old” (Isaiah 43:18) — and this from the prophet who has just recounted the exodus, so the command is not against remembering as such but against letting the old deliverance become the ceiling of expectation; the next verse says Behold, I will do a new thing. Ecclesiastes forbids nostalgia in blunter terms: “Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this” (Ecclesiastes 7:10). The verdict is not that the past was worse but that the question is unwise — it cannot be answered honestly and it does nothing but corrode the present. Paul uses the word for the discarded self: “put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts” (Ephesians 4:22), where conversation means the whole manner of life. And Revelation gives the last use, at the end of all sorrow: “there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away” (Revelation 21:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

What came before. Isaiah forbids making the old deliverance the ceiling of hope; Ecclesiastes calls nostalgia unwise enquiry; Paul makes the former manner of life a garment to put off; and in the end the former things pass away.

expand to see more

FORMER, a. [a comparative from forme, first.] Before in time; preceding another or something else in order of time.

2. Ancient; long past; as in former ages.

3. Mentioned before another; as, the former and the latter of two things.

4. Past, as opposed to present; as, my former state of life.

5. Former rain, the early rain of autumn, as distinguished from the latter rain of spring, Joel 2.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 43:18 — "Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old."

Ecclesiastes 7:10 — "Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this."

Ephesians 4:22 — "That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;"

Revelation 21:4 — "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."

Modern Corruption

The past is either idolised as a golden age — the enquiry Ecclesiastes calls unwise — or discarded entirely, so that a church loses the fathers, the confessions, and the memory of God's dealings.

expand to see more

Ecclesiastes 7:10 diagnoses a permanent temptation and does not flatter it. Asking why the former days were better is called unwise enquiry, and the reason is that the question is malformed: it assumes what it asks, it compares a remembered past with an experienced present, and it produces discontent without producing action. This is worth saying carefully, because a confessional Christian is committed to honouring the past — the Reformers, the Puritans, the 1689 — and there is a real difference between honouring fathers and pining for a decade. Isaiah 43:18 draws the same line from the other side: do not let what God did last time set the limit on what you expect him to do next. The opposite failure is the church that has cut itself loose from everything former, treating the fathers as irrelevant and the confessions as constraints. It always ends by rediscovering old heresies at great cost, because a body with no memory cannot recognise anything.

The principle to recover is Paul's image in Ephesians 4:22, where the former manner of life is a garment. Clothing is not the self; it is worn, and it can be taken off and left off. That is a mercy for anyone whose past is the thing he cannot get out from under. And the final word on the subject is Revelation 21:4, where the former things do not merely stop mattering, they pass away — death, sorrow, crying, and pain named individually and abolished, with God himself wiping the tears. Christians are not asked to pretend the former things were nothing. They are told what will become of them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rishon is first or former, from rosh, the head; qadmoni is ancient or of old. Greek proteros is former; protos, first.

expand to see more

Hebrew rishon (H7223) — first, former, foremost; the former things of Isaiah 43:18.

Hebrew qadmoni (H6931) — ancient, of old, eastern; the things of old.

Hebrew yoreh (H3138) — the former or early rain of autumn, which softened the ground for sowing.

Greek proteros (G4387) — former, earlier; the former conversation, Ephesians 4:22.

Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conversation; the whole walk that is put off.

Usage

"Of not capping hope with past mercies: remember ye not the former things (Isaiah 43:18)."

"Of nostalgia called unwise: say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? (Ecclesiastes 7:10)."

"Of the old life put off like a garment: put off concerning the former conversation the old man (Ephesians 4:22)."
